# Conﬁrming the Absence of Nuclear Warheads via Passive Gamma-Ray Measurements

Eric Lepowsky, Jihye Jeon, Alexander Glaser

Program on Science and Global Security, Princeton University

## Abstract

Arms-control agreements between the United States and Russia negoti-

ated after the end of the Cold War have imposed limits on the number of

deployed strategic nuclear weapons. Veriﬁcation of these agreements has re-

lied on onsite inspections, sometimes supported by radiation detection tech-

niques to conﬁrm the absence of a nuclear warhead when ambiguities arise.

So far, these measurements have sought to detect neutron emissions asso-

ciated with the presence of plutonium, but they would be inadequate for

uranium devices. In an eﬀort to oﬀer instruments that could be used to con-

ﬁrm the absence of both plutonium and uranium weapons, here we propose

an inspection system that uses passive gamma radiation detection techniques

only. Such a system would be particularly valuable for next-generation arms-

control agreements that limit total numbers of weapons and would involve

containerized items in storage. We conducted extensive Monte Carlo simu-

lations to support the development of a veriﬁcation protocol and detection

algorithm. We demonstrate the viability of the technique using standard lab-

oratory check sources and MCNP simulations for simpliﬁed conﬁgurations of

special nuclear material.

Keywords: Nuclear veriﬁcation, nuclear arms control, gamma spectroscopy

1. Background 1

There still exist more than 12,000 nuclear weapons in the world today [1]. 2

Only about 25% of these weapons are covered by the New START agreement 3

between Russia and the United States, which together still own more than 4

10,000 nuclear weapons. New START focuses only on deployed strategic 5

weapons and limits the number of such weapons to 1,550 on each side [2]. 6

It is widely believed that future arms-control agreements, either bilateral or 7

multilateral, would place limits on all weapons in the stockpiles, including 8

those in storage or slated for dismantlement, so that the growing gap be- 9

tween existing weapons and those captured by arms-control regimes can be 10

closed. Veriﬁcation approaches for such a future “all-warhead agreement” 11

often envision direct measurements on weapons to conﬁrm that they are in- 12

deed treaty accountable. Given the highly classiﬁed nature of these devices, 13

this approach raises important security concerns [3, 4, 5]. Several inspection 14

systems protecting sensitive information have been proposed over the years 15

[6], but none has been successfully deployed. Systems with information bar- 16

riers have been controversial in the past, and they are likely to remain so in 17

the future. 18

To resolve this dilemma, here, we examine the basic concept and pro- 19

totype of an inspection system that conﬁrms the absence of a nuclear war- 20

head, building on ideas developed as part of New START. Such an “absence 21

regime” could provide an “on-ramp” and lay the basis for more rigorous, but 22

also more intrusive, veriﬁcation approaches of future all-warhead agreements. 23

A follow-up regime could require positive identiﬁcation of treaty-accountable 24

2


<!-- Page 3 -->


items via serial numbers or unique identiﬁers. Finally, conﬁrmation measure- 25

ments may become necessary as part of an agreement that includes veriﬁed 26

dismantlement of nuclear weapons and enables deeper cuts in the arsenals. 27

An absence regime signiﬁcantly lowers the risk of revealing classiﬁed in- 28

formation since, in theory, no nuclear warheads should ever be inspected. 29

Instead, we assume the host simply declares objects on delivery systems or 30

in storage as “treaty limited” or “treaty accountable” items, and these will 31

be accepted as such; this is similar to the concept of “items declared as 32

weapons” proposed by the International Partnership for Disarmament Veri- 33

ﬁcation in a recent report [7, p. 5]. The dilemma arises when the number of 34

possible warheads or other treaty accountable items present at a site exceeds 35

the number of declared items. In this case, the host party needs to identify 36

which of these items are not treaty accountable. In most cases, the host may 37

be able to simply provide direct visual access to the item (e.g. by opening a 38

container) to conﬁrm its nature as a non-treaty-accountable item, but there 39

may be other situations where such a simple approach is not available. In 40

these cases, the inspector would be allowed to make radiation measurements 41

to conﬁrm the “absence of a nuclear weapon” or, more speciﬁcally, to conﬁrm 42

that the container does not contain suﬃcient amounts of plutonium or ura- 43

nium to make a nuclear weapon. Under an absence regime, nothing would 44

prevent a party from overdeclaring their warhead inventory, i.e., from having 45

fewer weapons in their arsenal than declared, but this is not a particularly 46

relevant non-compliance concern. 47

All ﬁssile materials are radioactive and can be detected by their gamma- 48

ray or neutron emissions [8, 9]. Although neutrons are often more readily 49

that all deployed Russian and U.S. strategic nuclear weapons contain pluto- 54

below uses passive gamma measurements only. It is therefore easily deploy- 65

weapons. 67

2. Estimating minimum radiation levels from a nuclear weapon 81

Plutonium and highly enriched uranium are the key ingredients in nuclear 82

weapons. The amounts and conﬁguration of these materials in weapons are 83

classiﬁed, and so are their radiation signatures. It is known, however, that 84

nuclear weapons contain kilogram quantities of plutonium or uranium, or 85

both. The United States has declassiﬁed the fact that, “hypothetically, a 86

mass of 4 kilograms of plutonium [...] is suﬃcient for one nuclear explosive 87

device” and that “all U.S. weapon pits that contain plutonium have at least 88

500 grams of plutonium” [14, p. 70]. Below, we use as reference values 89

the presence of at least one kilogram of weapon-grade plutonium (WPu) 90

containing 0.93 kg of Pu-239 or the presence of four kilograms of highly 91

enriched uranium (HEU) containing 3.72 kg of U-235 and 0.28 kg of U-238. 92

The 4:1 ratio we use here is based on the relative values of uranium-reﬂected 93

critical masses of HEU and plutonium. The inspected item is considered 94

treaty accountable if at least one of these limits is exceeded. Of course, other 95

values could be agreed upon by the parties considering deployment and use 96

of such a device for veriﬁcation purposes. 97

For gamma-ray detection, emission lines with relatively high energy and 98

intensity are preferable. Total emission rates are determined by the amounts 99

and half-lives of the relevant isotopes and their radioactive daughter prod- 100

their half-lives and assuming the isotopes are in secular equilibrium. In the 103

case of plutonium, we use a reference composition (DOE 3013) with a Pu-239 104

4. Veriﬁcation protocol for an absence-conﬁrmation system 222

There are four key steps in the proposed veriﬁcation protocol (visual- 223

ized in Figure 2) to apply the theory presented in Section 3: background 224

acquisition; characterization of a reference source; shielding estimate of the 225

container to be inspected using the reference source; and inspection of the 226

container itself. We envision that the host will be given the opportunity to 227

propose a measurement time for use with each of these steps because they 228

are aware of the content of the container and can estimate the minimum 229

measurement time for an unambiguous outcome. 230

In Step 1, the background is acquired. Ideally, the inspection should be 231

conducted in a low-background environment in order to minimize measure- 232

12


<!-- Page 13 -->

ment times. In principle, it should be in the interest of the host to provide 233

such an environment to expedite inspections and to avoid inconclusive out- 234

comes. Elevated backgrounds in the regions of interest will inevitably result 235

in longer measurement times. For best performance, the detector is placed in 236

a shielded collimator so that the system is primarily sensitive in the forward 237

direction, reducing overall background and susceptibility to other sources 238

that may be present nearby. 239

In Step 2, a reference source is placed on the “far side” of the setup; 240

this source will be used to estimate the amount of shielding present in the 241

inspected container, but its strength needs to be determined beforehand. 242

Here, we use the 661.7 keV line of cesium-137. The detection algorithm 243

veriﬁes the presence of an adequately strong calibration source by comparing 244

the count rates in those channels where the cesium peak is expected against 245

the previously measured background. If the source is deemed present and 246

suﬃciently strong, the inspection can proceed to measurements involving the 247

actual container. 248

In Step 3, the container selected for inspection is moved into position 249

between the detector and the reference source, and another measurement 250

with the reference source present is started. The reduction of the signal 251

compared to the previous measurement (Step 2) is used to estimate the 252

13


<!-- Page 14 -->


total eﬀective shielding in “millimeters of lead-equivalent.” Since we assume 253

that the containerized item is axially symmetric about its vertical axis, the 254

amount of shielding measured between the reference source and the detector 255

is twice the thickness between the center of the container and the detector. In 256

practice, it is not relevant whether the shielding is introduced by the content 257

of the container or the container itself, but it should be in the interest of 258

the host to work with containers that are standardized and do not introduce 259

extraneous amounts of shielding. 260

In Step 4, the reference source is removed, and the gamma emissions 261

originating from the container itself are measured. Along with the known 262

background and the estimated amount of shielding present, the detection 263

algorithm can now determine if emissions in the regions of interest (corre- 264

sponding to Pu-239 and U-238) are consistent with the absence of respective 265

threshold quantities of plutonium and uranium. 266

Algorithm 1 further demonstrates how the four acquired spectra are ana- 267

lyzed. The eﬀective shielding thickness is calculated using Eq. 2 based on the 268

spectra from Steps 2–4; the region of interest for the shielding estimate corre- 269

sponds to the reference source. The attenuation factor due to the estimated 270

shielding thickness for both regions of interest is then substituted into Eq. 271

1 to determine threshold signals for each material. The maximum shielding 272

thickness is also calculated, using the background spectrum and the theoreti- 273

cal counts of a notional bare source of the material, by combining Eq. 2 with 274

Eq. 3. The ﬁnal result is then deduced by simple comparisons with these 275

threshold values within each region of interest. If the inspection spectrum 276

exceeds 4 σ of the background, an anomaly is detected if the detected counts 277

14


<!-- Page 15 -->


also exceed the threshold signal. If the 4σ-test is not passed and the esti- 278

mated shielding thickness exceeds the calculated maximum shielding, then 279

the result is inconclusive. Otherwise, absence is conﬁrmed if the detected 280

counts are below the threshold signal or are less than 4 σ of the background 281

without exceeding the maximum shielding. 282

The device indicates the outcome of this analysis, for example, through 283

a number of LEDs: it can conﬁrm the absence of a nuclear weapon; it can 284

indicate the detection of an anomaly if radiation limits are exceeded; or it 285

can report an inconclusive measurement, which can be due to a combination 286

of high background levels, excessive shielding, and insuﬃcient measurement 287

time. Figure 3 shows a notional front panel of an inspection system that 288

follows the veriﬁcation protocol proposed here. 289

5. Experimental demonstration using check sources 290

Due to the diﬃculty of demonstrating the proposed concept with kilogram- 291

quantities of ﬁssile material, we examine its viability experimentally using 292

standard check sources. In general, such a modiﬁed system can serve as a 293

teaching tool and for prototyping purposes in standard laboratory settings. 294

Moreover, such a “benign” system can also be used for collaborations and 295

joint exercises aimed at developing new veriﬁcation approaches for arms- 296

control purposes. 297

We use barium-133 and cobalt-60 as substitutes for plutonium and ura- 298

nium, respectively. Speciﬁcally, we use barium-133 with prominent gamma 299

lines at 302.9 keV and 356.0 keV as a stand-in for plutonium-239; similarly, 300

we use one of the cobalt-60 peaks (1173.2 keV) to simulate uranium-238. 301

The fundamental detection algorithm is unchanged; the only parameters that 302

must be modiﬁed in order to switch between measurements in the ﬁeld versus 303

the laboratory are the locations of the regions of interest for the two relevant 304

isotopes, the corresponding attenuation coeﬃcients, and the threshold activ- 305

ities (or total detector counts in the respective region of interest) to indicate 306

an anomaly. 307

For the laboratory setup, we use a collimated Mirion/Canberra NaI de- 308

tector (Model 802) connected to an Osprey Digital MCA Tube Base [19, 20] 309

and a reduced standoﬀdistance of 20 cm in order to expedite the measure- 310

ments. The total activity of the barium-133 and cobalt-60 sources at the 311

time of measurement was approximately 1.4 µCi and 0.9 µCi, respectively. 312

The results of an experimental demonstration of the veriﬁcation protocol are 313

shown in Figure 4 and summarized in Table 2. For this particular case of 314

7. Conclusion and outlook 347

For thirty years, international research and development eﬀorts have 348

sought to develop inspection systems that can conﬁrm the authenticity of 349

a nuclear weapon to support the veriﬁcation regime of a future arms-control 350

treaty. With few exceptions, little progress has been made toward certifying 351

and authenticating such candidate systems because of security concerns as- 352

sociated with such inspections. This article starts out with the observation 353

that inspections of nuclear weapons may in fact not be necessary, at least not 354

initially. Instead, we follow the proposition of simply accepting as weapons 355

all “items declared as weapons” by the host. Veriﬁcation of such an all- 356

warhead agreement would be drastically simpliﬁed, but it could still require 357

instruments that can conﬁrm that some containerized items (ﬂagged by an 358

inspector) are in fact not treaty accountable, even when the host cannot oﬀer 359

visual access to these items. 360

To support this process, here, we have proposed and demonstrated a mea- 361

surement approach that relies exclusively on passive gamma measurements 362

using a low-resolution (sodium-iodide) detector. The system would be easily 363

deployable in the ﬁeld and able to conﬁrm the absence of both plutonium- 364

based and uranium-based weapons. In a veriﬁcation regime based on absence 365

measurements, no weapons should ever be part of an inspection, and safety 366

and security concerns would therefore be dramatically reduced. The proto- 367

col involves only a small number of basic steps with the only non-standard 368

requirement being the use of a check source (e.g. Cs-137) with an activity in 369

the 1 mCi range. 370

Our results show that the absence of a threshold quantity of plutonium 371

23


<!-- Page 24 -->


or uranium can be conﬁrmed within minutes, even if a shielded container is 372

inspected. One important feature of the proposed protocol is the ability of 373

the host to propose a measurement time, which expedites inspections and 374

can proactively avoid inconclusive inspection outcomes. No gamma gross- 375

count or spectral information is ever revealed to the inspector, only the ﬁnal 376

inspection result, i.e., absence conﬁrmed, inconclusive, or anomaly detected. 377

Overall, we ﬁnd that absence measurements show great promise in overcom- 378

ing the technical challenges of veriﬁed deeper cuts in the nuclear arsenals. 379

For further development and demonstration purposes, we also oﬀer a min- 380

imally modiﬁed algorithm for use with standard check sources using Ba-133 381

and Co-60 as stand-ins for Pu-239 and U-238, respectively. The performance 382

of the inspection system and the viability of the overall veriﬁcation approach 383

can be evaluated using such a system, which could also support domestic or 384

international inspection exercises. The construction of a portable version of 385

the system is straightforward, as it may be possible to use commercially avail- 386

able hardware. Field-testing of such a system could help develop the concept 387

further and enable red-teaming of the proposed veriﬁcation protocol. 388
